goal: Snake game on an Arduino Uno: an 8x8 MAX7219 LED matrix module (DIN on D11, CS on D10, CLK on D13, VCC to 5V, GND) shows the snake and the food, and a KY-023 analog joystick (VRx on A0, VRy on A1, SW on D2 using INPUT_PULLUP, +5V, GND) steers it. The snake grows when it eats, and the game restarts when it hits itself or a wall; pressing the joystick restarts it too. Use the LedControl library.

plan.title: Arduino Uno Snake Game
plan.summary: Build a Snake game using an 8×8 MAX7219 LED matrix and an analog joystick. Move the joystick to steer toward the food; the snake grows when it eats, and the game restarts after a collision or a joystick-button press.
plan.final_result: The finished breadboard has the matrix input header at rows 10–14 and the joystick header at rows 40–44, with twelve wires connecting both modules to the Uno and shared power rails. With the supplied sketch running, a three-pixel snake moves across the display toward blinking food. Eating adds one segment; hitting a wall or the snake's body restarts the game, as does pressing the joystick. Filling all 64 cells starts a new game.

tests.title: Test the 8x8 LED matrix display
tests.what_it_tests: This confirms that power, ground, and SPI communication wires to the MAX7219 matrix are functioning properly.
tests.code: void writeCmd(byte r, byte d) { digitalWrite(10, LOW); shiftOut(11, 13, MSBFIRST, r); shiftOut(11, 13, MSBFIRST, d); digitalWrite(10, HIGH); } void setup() { pinMode(10, OUTPUT); pinMode(11, OUTPUT); pinMode(13, OUTPUT); writeCmd(0x0F, 0x00); writeCmd(0x0C, 0x01); writeCmd(0x0B, 0x07); writeCmd(0x0A, 0x02); writeCmd(0x09, 0x00); for (byte r = 1; r <= 8; r++) { writeCmd(r, (1 << (r - 1)) | (1 << (8 - r))); } } void loop() { }
tests.expect: Plug in the USB cable and upload this sketch. An 'X' pattern should light up steadily across the 8x8 LED matrix.
tests.if_not: If no LEDs light up or random dots flicker, check the power and ground rails from Steps 4 and 5, verify the 5V jumper in Step 6 (row 10, column f) and ground jumper in Step 7 (row 11, column f), and ensure the data lines in Step 8 (pin 11 to row 12), Step 9 (pin 10 to row 13), and Step 10 (pin 13 to row 14) are firmly inserted and not swapped.

tests.title: Test the joystick analog axes
tests.what_it_tests: This confirms that the joystick is powered and its horizontal and vertical analog signals reach the Arduino.
tests.code: void setup() { Serial.begin(9600); } void loop() { Serial.print("X: "); Serial.print(analogRead(A0)); Serial.print(" | Y: "); Serial.println(analogRead(A1)); delay(300); }
tests.expect: Plug in the USB cable and upload this sketch. Open the Serial Monitor at 9600 baud. You should see continuous readings with X and Y values around 512 at rest, shifting smoothly toward 0 and 1023 as you deflect the joystick stick.
tests.if_not: If both readings stay at 0 or 1023 regardless of movement, check the ground jumper in Step 11 (row 40, column f) and 5V jumper in Step 12 (row 41, column f). If only one axis fails to respond, check Step 13 (A0 to row 42, column f) or Step 14 (A1 to row 43, column f).

safety: Keep USB and every other power source disconnected while placing components or changing wiring.
Check the actual printed module pin labels before insertion. Module variants can reverse header order; do not apply power if the labels do not match this plan.
Use only the matrix input header containing DIN. Leave its output header unconnected.
The positive rail is 5V, not VIN or 3.3V. Never connect the positive rail to the ground rail.
Use a MAX7219 module with its onboard current-setting resistor and decoupling capacitors fitted. The sketch uses low brightness to limit USB current demand.
Do not push module bodies down against jumper wires or bend headers to force a fit. This placement requires the stated breadboard-compatible header geometry.
Support the overhanging joystick body from underneath when pressing it so its header and the breadboard are not strained.
Power this build from the Uno USB connection only; no separate matrix supply or external voltage is needed.

part_guide.uno: The blue-green Arduino board with a USB-B socket runs the game. Identify its connections by the printed header labels, not their positions in the simplified model.
part_guide.matrix: The square array of 64 LEDs on a MAX7219 module displays the snake and blinking food. Use the input header marked DIN, not the output header marked DOUT.
part_guide.joystick: The module with a movable black thumb stick provides two analog steering signals. Pressing the stick closes its SW button and restarts the game.
part_guide.ground_supply: This black wire connects Arduino GND to the ground rail along the top edge. Both modules share this electrical reference.
part_guide.power_supply: This red wire connects Arduino 5V to the inner red positive rail along the top edge. It supplies both modules.
part_guide.matrix_power: This red wire carries 5V from the positive rail to the matrix VCC row.
part_guide.matrix_ground: This black wire connects the matrix GND row to the shared ground rail.
part_guide.matrix_data: This green wire carries display data from Arduino pin 11 to matrix DIN.
part_guide.matrix_select: This yellow wire connects Arduino pin 10 to matrix CS, telling the display when to accept a command.
part_guide.matrix_clock: This blue wire connects Arduino pin 13 to matrix CLK, timing the display data.
part_guide.joystick_ground: This black wire connects the joystick GND row to the shared ground rail.
part_guide.joystick_power: This red wire supplies 5V to the joystick's +5V row.
part_guide.joystick_x: This orange wire carries the joystick's VRx voltage to analog input A0 for horizontal steering.
part_guide.joystick_y: This purple wire carries the joystick's VRy voltage to analog input A1 for vertical steering.
part_guide.joystick_switch: This white wire connects joystick SW to digital pin 2. The sketch uses the Uno's internal pull-up resistor, so no separate button resistor is needed.

assumptions: No existing parts or bench layout were supplied, so all required hardware is added.

Use modules with pre-soldered breadboard-compatible male headers. This layout requires the matrix INPUT header to read VCC, GND, DIN, CS, CLK in increasing row order, and the joystick header to read GND, +5V, VRx, VRy, SW in increasing row order.

Before buying or inserting modules, confirm that their header geometry allows the bodies to overhang outward beyond column j while leaving column f accessible. If the header order or geometry differs, do not force the module into this layout; obtain a revised placement plan.
The module bodies intentionally overhang the lower breadboard edge; only their header pins plug into the breadboard. Support the joystick body from underneath when pressing it.
The outer top rail, above column a, is the blue negative ground rail. The adjacent inner top rail is the red positive 5V rail. Both are assumed continuous along all 63 rows.
The MAX7219 module includes its normal current-setting resistor and supply-decoupling components. No individual LED resistors are needed.
The Uno is represented by the specified 55 × 28 × 7 mm scene template, not its actual 68.6 × 53.4 mm PCB outline; terminal anchors are symbolic.
Joystick axis direction and matrix orientation vary between modules. The sketch includes axis-inversion and display-transform constants so their orientation can be corrected without rewiring.
Install the LedControl library through the Arduino IDE Library Manager before compiling the supplied sketch.

placements.where: Arduino digital header socket labelled 2
row 44, column f (right of the centre gap)

steps.check: A white wire runs from Uno digital pin 2 to f44, sharing the row with joystick SW at j44. The finished circuit contains exactly twelve jumper wires.

plan.final_result: The finished breadboard has the matrix input header at rows 10–14 and the joystick header at rows 40–44, with twelve wires connecting both modules to the Uno and shared power rails. With the supplied sketch running, a three-pixel snake moves across the display toward blinking food. Eating adds one segment; hitting a wall or the snake's body restarts the game, as does pressing the joystick. Filling all 64 cells starts a new game.
safety: Keep USB and every other power source disconnected while placing components or changing wiring.
Check the actual printed module pin labels before insertion. Module variants can reverse header order; do not apply power if the labels do not match this plan.
Use only the matrix input header containing DIN. Leave its output header unconnected.
The positive rail is 5V, not VIN or 3.3V. Never connect the positive rail to the ground rail.
Use a MAX7219 module with its onboard current-setting resistor and decoupling capacitors fitted. The sketch uses low brightness to limit USB current demand.
Do not push module bodies down against jumper wires or bend headers to force a fit. This placement requires the stated breadboard-compatible header geometry.
Support the overhanging joystick body from underneath when pressing it so its header and the breadboard are not strained.
Power this build from the Uno USB connection only; no separate matrix supply or external voltage is needed.

tests.title: Test the 8x8 LED matrix display
tests.what_it_tests: This confirms that power, ground, and SPI communication wires to the MAX7219 matrix are functioning properly.
tests.code: void writeCmd(byte r, byte d) { digitalWrite(10, LOW); shiftOut(11, 13, MSBFIRST, r); shiftOut(11, 13, MSBFIRST, d); digitalWrite(10, HIGH); } void setup() { pinMode(10, OUTPUT); pinMode(11, OUTPUT); pinMode(13, OUTPUT); writeCmd(0x0F, 0x00); writeCmd(0x0C, 0x01); writeCmd(0x0B, 0x07); writeCmd(0x0A, 0x02); writeCmd(0x09, 0x00); for (byte r = 1; r <= 8; r++) { writeCmd(r, (1 << (r - 1)) | (1 << (8 - r))); } } void loop() { }
tests.expect: Plug in the USB cable and upload this sketch. An 'X' pattern should light up steadily across the 8x8 LED matrix.
tests.if_not: If no LEDs light up or random dots flicker, check the power and ground rails from Steps 4 and 5, verify the 5V jumper in Step 6 (row 10, column f) and ground jumper in Step 7 (row 11, column f), and ensure the data lines in Step 8 (pin 11 to row 12), Step 9 (pin 10 to row 13), and Step 10 (pin 13 to row 14) are firmly inserted and not swapped.

tests.title: Test the joystick analog axes
tests.what_it_tests: This confirms that the joystick is powered and its horizontal and vertical analog signals reach the Arduino.
tests.code: void setup() { Serial.begin(9600); } void loop() { Serial.print("X: "); Serial.print(analogRead(A0)); Serial.print(" | Y: "); Serial.println(analogRead(A1)); delay(300); }
tests.expect: Plug in the USB cable and upload this sketch. Open the Serial Monitor at 9600 baud. You should see continuous readings with X and Y values around 512 at rest, shifting smoothly toward 0 and 1023 as you deflect the joystick stick.
tests.if_not: If both readings stay at 0 or 1023 regardless of movement, check the ground jumper in Step 11 (row 40, column f) and 5V jumper in Step 12 (row 41, column f). If only one axis fails to respond, check Step 13 (A0 to row 42, column f) or Step 14 (A1 to row 43, column f).
